message.content: {"thought": "Current hardware: 32 WS chiplets, 16384 CU (max), 8192 buf, DRAM BW=64, NoP BW=128, micro_batch=2, tp=32. The search space allows DRAM BW up to 256 and NoP BW up to 512. The critical-path tail layers (norm2, res2, GeLU, res1) have both significant DRAM time and NoC time. The aggregate energy is 42.7% memory, 33.8% communication, 22.6% compute. The monetary cost is 52.8% compute, 39.4% OS, 7.9% IO. The historical NoP increase on 16 chiplets failed (MC 237.6 -> 418.3, +76%), but on 32 chiplets the IO cost share is only 7.9%, so doubling NoP BW would have a smaller relative MC impact. However, the critical-path tail layers have more DRAM time than NoC time for norm2 (1.29ms vs 0.95ms) and GeLU (3.89ms vs 2.65ms), while res2 has more NoC time (1.97ms vs 1.52ms). Increasing DRAM BW from 64 to 128 would reduce the memory component of these critical-path layers. The IO cost share is 7.9%, and DRAM BW is part of IO cost. Let me consider increasing DRAM BW to 128. The monetary cost impact would be modest (IO is only 7.9% of total), and the latency reduction from faster DRAM access on the critical-path tail layers could improve the critical end time and potentially reduce energy. Let me also consider that the FFN1 compute-bound layers (68.4% of time) are already at max compute_units, so the only way to reduce their latency is to increase chiplet count or change dataflow type. Increasing chiplet count to 64 would double compute capacity but also increase MC significantly (OS cost is 39.4%). The historical case shows that going from 16 to 32 chiplets improved objective by 12% despite MC doubling. Going from 32 to 64 would further increase MC. Let me check the compare_search_states to see the trajectory and understand what moves have been tried.", "action": "tool", "tool": {"name": "compare_search_states", "arguments": {"include_history": true, "history_limit": 5, "include_hardware": true}}}
